# Predicting the next human utterance: a first step toward learner simulation with TutorMoments

A tutoring model chooses what to say. A learner model predicts how a person might respond. Separating those two problems is important: an observational prediction model is not evidence that changing a tutor's words will improve learning. We test a narrow observable outcome on real tutoring conversations before considering full generative simulation.

![462 sessions and 57,912 eligible turn pairs](/assets/research/h27-cover.svg)

## Real data, research-only processing

Ai2's [TutorMoments-Preview](https://huggingface.co/datasets/allenai/tutormoments-preview) contains 462 real tutoring sessions, 520 teacher-annotated benchmark moments and 7,280 AI replay attempts. We use only the real transcript subset, pinned at revision 3bb0c104d65e29facffca7ba864ef10fa22d0e78. The [official explanation](https://allenai.org/blog/tutormoments), [code](https://github.com/allenai/tutormoments) and [responsible-use guidelines](https://allenai.org/responsible-use) informed the design. The data is licensed CC BY 4.0 and intended for research and education. It involves minors, and deidentification is imperfect. No reidentification, individual psychological profiling, external API inference, raw text publication, or weight sharing was performed. Only aggregate results and code are retained for sharing; the raw transcript file downloaded in this run was deleted after replay.

## Defining a measurable outcome

We select immediately adjacent tutor-to-student turns with nonempty text and an earlier nonempty student turn. A binary target records whether the next student utterance contains at most three regex-defined words. It is not a label for comprehension, engagement or emotion. We excluded 263 otherwise eligible adjacent pairs lacking the required context or text and obtained 57,912 pairs.

![Student-group split and observable features](/assets/research/h27-method.svg)

A fixed SHA-256 assignment partitions student pseudonym groups, never using the identifiers as model features. Train comprises 293 sessions, 122 groups and 37,308 pairs; validation 74 sessions, 32 groups and 8,369 pairs; test 95 sessions, 44 groups and 12,235 pairs. Student groups do not overlap, although tutors may overlap. Earlier research H23 used part of the same public corpus, so this is not a research-program-wide untouched external test.

We fit logistic regression with five nonidentifying features: tutor word count, question-mark presence, previous student word count, previous short-turn indicator, and conversation position. Counts and position use log1p; standardization statistics come from training only. Four L2 regularization values (0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1) are selected by validation Brier score. Comparators include a training prior, a conditional frequency based on the last short-turn indicator, a history model, a tutor-feature-plus-position model, and the full model. No future utterance, identifier, demographic or text embedding enters the predictor.

Brier score averages squared differences between predicted probabilities and binary outcomes. Lower is better; this measures probability prediction, not learning.

## Results

![Measured test Brier scores](/assets/research/h27-results.svg)

| Model | Test Brier | Test NLL |
|---|---:|---:|
| Prior | 0.247179 | 0.687500 |
| Persistence | 0.240571 | 0.674054 |
| History | 0.238853 | 0.670570 |
| Tutor only + position | 0.246196 | 0.685534 |
| Full | 0.237884 | 0.668665 |

The full model reduces Brier score by approximately 3.76% relative to the prior. Its advantage over history is only 0.000969. A paired bootstrap over held-out student groups (2,000 resamples) gives a 95% percentile interval of [-0.013791,-0.004703] for Full minus Prior and [-0.002768,0.000814] for Full minus History. The latter includes zero. Additional predictive value from tutor features beyond history is therefore not established. The interval reflects sampling variation under this cluster bootstrap, not uncertainty across providers or populations.

A replay produced byte-identical aggregate JSON. A separate standard-library calculation reproduced Brier and NLL for all five models within 1e-12. Seven aggregate validation tests passed in normal and optimized Python. These are engineering checks, not independent peer review.

## Implications for Manager

Recent observations can improve a simple prior, but the teacher-feature ablation illustrates why a stronger baseline matters. Predicting short replies does not simulate their content or establish causal intervention effects. Full learner-turn generation, independent external testing, and real learning outcomes remain unmeasured. We do not transfer these fitted weights or learner data into Manager or a product. Only the evaluation design is a candidate for reuse under separate governance. Outstanding work is tracked in [issue #821](https://github.com/Daisuke134/anicca-ops/issues/821).
